en: Record of the Transmission of the Dharma Jewel, with Preface,
composed by □ Mo (style name Fangming) of Jingzhao.
I bow my head to the Good Spiritual Friend (*kalyāṇamitra*), who is able to cause one to protect the fundamental mind, just as [a lily blooms] within turbid water.
The power of the jewel suddenly purifies what appears; This is why I have established this record.
May this dharma of successive transmission continue until the end of the future, Widely opening up the Buddha’s knowledge and vision. Preface:
That which is attained by the Dharma-Buddha of my true Dharma-body is apart from the verbal expressions of all transformation-buddhas and does not rely upon written characters; rather,
this Gate of True Suchness is transmitted solely through the self-awakening of the realized mind.
Therefore, the treatise states:
"All dharmas, from the very beginning, are free from the characteristics of verbal expression and free from the characteristics of names."
Free from mental objects and signs,
it is ultimately equal,
without any change or variation.
It cannot be destroyed;
because it is solely this one mind, it is called True Suchness (*tathatā*).
It is also said:
Regarding the realization of the awakening mind:
from the Stage of Pure Mind up to the ultimate stage,
what realm is realized?
That which is called *tathatā* (suchness) is described as an object (*viṣaya*) in dependence upon the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*).
However, for this realized one, there is no such object;
the wisdom of *tathatā* alone is termed the *dharmakāya*.
Furthermore, as stated in the Sūtras:
"The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, alone in a quiet place, awakens through self-observation and investigation without depending on others;
free from the delusions of views, he ascends higher and higher, entering the stage of the Tathāgata."
This is called the noble wisdom of self-awakening.
Therefore, if one does not attain the transmission of the Unsurpassed Vehicle within the ground of the mind,
who could possibly enter the realm of reality?
Formerly, in the Preface to the *Dhyāna-sūtra* by the Venerable Huiyuan of Mount Lu, it was stated:
"The Buddha entrusted [the teaching] to Ānanda;
Ānanda transmitted it to Madhyāntika."
Maudgalyāyana transmitted [the teachings] to Śāṇavāsa;
thus we know that the ear does not fall to the ground after death—this depends on the person being ultimate.
How could this be merely a matter of binding oneself to cause and effect or investigating the meaning of words?
Is there that which can be entered?
That which is called the "penetration of the essence" (*zongtong*) in the *Sūtras* refers to the supreme path realized through one's own personal attainment.
They remain far removed from the conceptual constructions of speech and letters,
proceeding toward the outflow-free realm (*anāsrava-dhātu*) and the stage of self-realization (*pratyātma-bhūmi*),
wherein they are personally characterized by being free from all marks of false awakening.
Having subdued all externalists and the hosts of Māras,
the light of the path of self-awakening radiates forth;
this is called the characteristic of the ultimate principle (zōng-tōng).
This is the realm of ultimate truth;
it is believed that one cannot enter it through mere discursive reasoning.
There are those who have set out from India and traveled this way to this land.
Is there such a person as Bodhidharma?
At that time, he was transmitted by one of superior wisdom in China.
Yet, does he point toward the true realm?
Is it not as if those who have lost their way in youth are suddenly made to turn back toward themselves?
It is also like a great bright torch being lit in a dark room—how can it be described in words?
Subsequently, as the nature of his realization was exceptional and transcendent, he rose far above others.
Some, being preoccupied with what they had previously practiced, sought no superior wisdom;
thus, when the Great Master suddenly transmitted it to them, they were rarely capable of receiving it upon their heads.
Only Huikai of the Eastern Wei sought it with his very life, and the Great Master passed it on to him before departing.
Huike transmitted [the Dharma] to Sengcan;
Sengcan transmitted it to Daoxin;
and Daoxin transmitted it to Hongren.
Hongren transmitted the Dharma to Faru;
Faru reached the stage of Great Penetration (Dàtōng).
Since the time of Bodhidharma, these successive teachers and disciples have opened the Way.
All were skilled at using expedient means to realize the truth within the mind;
whatever words they uttered were concise and free from attachment.
Now, among humans there may be texts titled *Dharmapada* or *Dharmasaṃgraha*.
It is likely that at that time, practitioners took the words they had personally realized as authentic treatises and treasured them;
these were also frequently erroneous.
As for those who attained transcendental realization through successive transmission:
Once this has been attained within the mind, there is no room for sound;
how then could speech or written characters find a place between?
Indeed, one who does not perceive the ultimate cannot [attain it].
One should point to the small to clarify the great and the provisional. If,
according to worldly teachings, there were those who refined elixirs (*zhen dan*) to ascend to heaven in broad daylight,
they must have obtained the manual techniques transmitted by the bodies of immortals (*xianren*) before the refinement could succeed.
If one relies on the jade-scripted writings of the "Bi" character, one will ultimately be overwhelmed by surging waves and vast confusion.
Within this world, even a single conditioned phenomenon remains subject to necessity;
how much more so the unsurpassed True Doctrine, which can certainly not be bound by words and speech?
Therefore, this Way is subtle and profound, and its gateway is rarely found.
Although the Dharma does not rely on the person but on the meaning, and does not rely on the words but on the principle,
how can one ever find a true spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra) upon whom to rely?
Now, this Supreme Person (zhiren) is beyond comparison and difficult to name; perhaps it is to instruct the unenlightened or because the day is drawing to a close.
For this reason, I have now composed this brief record.
As for those who have successively transmitted the Dharma since the time of Bodhidharma:
I have recorded these in sequence to form one volume titled *The Chronicle of the Transmission of Treasures*.

I shall now append here what I have personally seen of famous sites and the regions where he transformed beings, as well as those matters within my own hearing and sight that are clearly documented in written records.
Subsequently, as [the Master] merged into oneness with him, the biographies became simplified;
as for his realization of the holy path, there is nothing that can be expressed in words.
I shall arrange the portraits of his physical likeness here as a supplementary record for future generations.
Yet, as this Way has been transmitted through successive generations, it remains profoundly serene;
in the state of the true emptiness of the dharma-realm, all traces of form naturally vanish.
Thus, throughout one's entire life, no extraordinary signs manifest.
I have heard no records of their spiritual traces, and for this reason I have omitted them.
This is like wiping one's face with the hem of one's sleeve; though it may be bright and moist, it is not taken [as a source].
Furthermore, from after Bodhidharma until the Sui and Tang dynasties...
As for those who possessed lofty awakening, profound transcendence, and deep penetration into the Perfect and Sudden [teachings]—
could such individuals have been absent in any age?
Since they did not belong to the lineage of formal transmission, they are listed separately in this biographical section.
This illustrates that this Dharma-gate has many patriarchs. They are: Śramaṇa Bodhidharma of Shaolin Temple on Mount Song at Dongwei;

Śramaṇa Huiké of Shaolin Temple on Mount Song during the Northern Qi; Śramaṇa Sengcan of Mount Suwam; Śramaṇa Daoxin of Dongshan Temple on Mount Shuangfeng during the Tang; Śramaṇa Hongren of Dongshan Temple on Mount Shuangfeng during the Tang; Śramaṇa Faru of Shaolin Temple on Mount Song during the Tang; and Śramaṇa Shenxiu of Wangquan Temple in Dangyang during the Tang. Bodhidharma was of Brahmin lineage, the third son of the King of Southern India. His spiritual faculties were transcendent and awakened; he transmitted the self-realized noble wisdom (*pratyātma-āryajñāna*).
He extensively opened the Buddha’s knowledge and vision for humans and devas.
For the sake of us people of China, he brought [the teachings] across the ocean and over high mountains; at that time, those who knew them were rare.
Only Dao-yu and Hui-ke, whose long-held aspirations were secretly in accord, sought them with exhaustive diligence.
In the sixth year, the Master’s resolve was set upon attaining profound realization.
The Great Master, speaking with composure, asked him:
"Are you able to sacrifice your body and life for the sake of the Dharma?"
According to the *Yuanjue jing dashu chao*, Huikě severed his own arm to verify his sincerity;

however, the *Xu zhuan* states that he had his arm lopped off by bandits, which is likely a contemporary error. Thereafter, [the Master] began to secretly develop and guide him through skillful means.
Thus, both teacher and disciple were fully enlightened.
